tasks.prompt: Order the steps for scoring and ranking mains for the next flushing cycle.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: ranking all candidate mains for next year program.

cards.label: Score each main for residual history, complaint history and water age
Add a score factor for main material and age where records support it
Total the scores and rank the mains from highest need to lowest
Match the ranked list to the crew time and water budget available
Set the cut line and list the mains deferred to the following cycle
File the scoring sheet so next year ranking starts from this record

tasks.explanation: Scoring makes the priority order defensible and repeatable. Matching the ranked list to real crew and water budgets prevents an approved program that cannot be finished, and filing the scores keeps the reasoning for deferred mains on record.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting up a storage turnover management program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: all storage facilities in the system.

cards.label: Record the usable volume and normal level range for each facility
Calculate the current turnover time for each facility from demand records
Set a target turnover range for each facility by season
Adjust level setpoints and pump controls to meet the targets
Monitor water age indicators such as residuals at facility outlets
Review turnover monthly and report facilities outside target

tasks.explanation: Turnover targets are meaningless until current turnover is calculated from real demand. Setpoints are the control that achieves the target, outlet residuals show whether age is actually improving, and monthly review keeps storage from drifting back to old habits.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting up a storage inspection program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: program for elevated tanks, standpipes and ground reservoirs.

cards.label: Inventory all storage facilities with type, age and coating history
Set inspection intervals for external, internal and coating assessments
Create checklists covering structure, coating, vents, overflows and security
Schedule the first cycle so the oldest and poorest condition facilities come first
Assign qualified inspectors or contract the internal inspections
File inspection reports and link deficiencies to work orders

tasks.explanation: The inventory and condition history decide the inspection order. Checklists keep every facility judged on the same items, qualified inspection matters most for internal work, and linking reports to work orders ensures findings become repairs.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for planning a reservoir cleaning cycle.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one ground reservoir due for cleaning.

cards.label: Review the last cleaning record and recent sediment and quality results
Schedule the cleaning for a low demand period and confirm alternate storage
Notify operations and customers who could be affected by the outage
Drain and clean the reservoir under the confined space and disinfection procedures
Inspect the interior during cleaning and record coating and structure condition
Disinfect, refill, sample and return the reservoir only after results are accepted

tasks.explanation: Cleaning is scheduled around demand and alternate storage so supply is never at risk. The drained reservoir is also the best inspection opportunity, and return to service waits for accepted samples, not just for the cleaning to finish.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing storage level controls after repeated overflow alarms.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one elevated tank with overflow alarms in the past month.

cards.label: Review alarm records and the tank level trend for each overflow event
Check the level sensor readings against a manual level measurement
Inspect altitude valve or pump control settings that fill the tank
Correct the sensor or control fault found
Test the controls through a full fill cycle while watching levels
Record the fault, the correction and the test result in the facility log

tasks.explanation: Alarm history shows the pattern, but the sensor must be proven against a manual measurement before controls are blamed. The fault is corrected, then proven by a watched fill cycle, because an untested fix for an overflow is only a hope.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a winter ice management program for elevated storage.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: elevated tanks in a cold prairie winter.

cards.label: Review last winter ice records and any damage found at spring inspection
Confirm circulation or mixing measures are operating before freeze up
Set winter level ranges that reduce ice formation risk
Monitor tank levels and temperatures through the coldest periods
Inspect accessible vents, ladders and overflow for ice blockage after cold snaps
Record ice conditions and plan any spring repairs from the findings

tasks.explanation: Ice management starts before freeze up, because circulation must be running before ice forms. Winter level ranges and monitoring limit damage during cold snaps, and spring repairs are planned from recorded conditions rather than rediscovered damage.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a storage facility security and access review.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: all storage sites in an annual security review.

cards.label: Visit each site and check fencing, gates, locks and signage
Check hatch and vent screens and locks for damage or gaps
Review the access log and key control records for each site
Repair or replace failed security hardware found during the visits
Update the site security checklist and the key inventory
Report the review and any unresolved risks to the supervisor

tasks.explanation: Security is verified by visiting sites, not by assuming last year condition holds. Hatches and vents protect water quality directly, key control shows who can enter, and unresolved risks are reported rather than left in a checklist.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for investigating high water age in a low demand storage zone.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one reservoir serving a slow growing area with falling residuals.

cards.label: Confirm low residuals at the reservoir outlet and in the served area
Calculate the current turnover from level records and zone demand
Check whether operating levels can be lowered without risking fire storage
Trial the lower level range and monitor outlet residuals
If age remains high, evaluate mixing or a smaller active volume option
Record the decision and the new operating range for the facility

tasks.explanation: Low outlet residuals confirm the complaint is a storage age problem. Turnover calculation quantifies it, a level trial is the lowest cost remedy and is monitored before capital options are considered, and the chosen range is recorded for all shifts.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps in the program response to a storage overflow event.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one tank overflow reported overnight.

cards.label: Confirm the overflow has stopped and check the site for erosion or property damage
Record the level trend and the control settings at the time of the event
Notify the supervisor and document any water loss volume estimate
Inspect the level controls and alarms for the cause
Repair the fault and test the high level alarm before returning to normal operation
File the event report and add the facility to closer monitoring

tasks.explanation: The site is made safe and damage is recorded first. The cause is found in controls and alarms, not assumed, the alarm is tested before normal operation resumes, and closer monitoring follows because one overflow often repeats.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for planning the decommissioning of an old standpipe.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: planning stage for removing a standpipe from service.

cards.label: Confirm the standpipe is no longer needed for storage or fire protection with system records
Plan how demand and fire flow will be met without the facility
Notify affected customers and the fire department of the planned removal date
Drain the facility and disconnect it from the distribution system
Remove or secure the structure under the approved work plan
Update system maps, storage records and the asset register

tasks.explanation: Need is proven from records before a facility is retired, and replacement supply and fire protection are planned before notification. Disconnection precedes structural work, and closing the records prevents future crews from planning around a facility that no longer exists.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for preparing the annual storage condition report.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: report covering all storage facilities.

cards.label: Compile the year inspection findings and photographs for each facility
Summarize cleaning, repairs and overflow or ice events for the year
Rank facilities by condition and by consequence of failure
Estimate the next five year inspection, cleaning and repair needs
Identify any facility needing capital assessment in the coming year
Present the report to management and file it with the asset records

tasks.explanation: The annual report combines inspections and events so condition trends are visible. Ranking by condition and consequence directs money to the facility whose failure would hurt most, and the five year view prevents surprise capital needs.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting up a duty and standby pump rotation program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one booster station with three similar pumps.

cards.label: Record run hours for each pump from the station log
Set the rotation order so run hours equalize across the pumps
Program or schedule the lead pump change to follow the rotation
Run each standby pump under load during the first rotation cycle
Check for vibration, leaks and abnormal noise during each test run
Record the rotation and run hours in the station log

tasks.explanation: Rotation starts from actual run hours so equalization is real. Standby pumps are proven under load, not just started, because a pump that cannot carry load is not a standby, and the log keeps the rotation honest.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for responding to a high wet well or high discharge pressure alarm at a booster station.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one night alarm at an unattended booster station.

cards.label: Acknowledge the alarm and check station pressures and levels remotely if available
Attend the station and check for flooding, leaks or a closed valve condition
Check which pumps are running and compare discharge pressure with normal
Switch to the standby pump if the duty pump is the cause
Restore normal operation and confirm pressures return to range
Record the alarm, cause and actions in the station log and notify the supervisor

tasks.explanation: Remote checks shape the response before arrival, but the cause is confirmed at the station. Switching to standby restores supply while the fault is isolated, and the log plus notification close the event for the next shift.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a pump efficiency spot check at a booster station.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one duty pump checked against its expected performance.

cards.label: Record suction and discharge pressures and calculate the pump head
Measure or read the pump flow from the station meter
Compare the head and flow point with the pump expected performance record
Check for throttled valves, wear signs and abnormal power draw
Report any shortfall and schedule detailed testing if performance is low
File the spot check with the station performance history

tasks.explanation: Head and flow must be measured together, because either alone cannot locate the pump on its curve. Valve and wear checks explain common shortfalls, and filing the check builds the history that shows gradual decline.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for restarting a booster station after a power outage.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: station restart after utility power returns.

cards.label: Confirm power is stable and check the station for damage or flooding
Check pump and valve positions against the normal lineup
Start the lead pump and watch suction and discharge pressures rise
Check for leaks, abnormal noise and correct rotation indications
Start additional pumps only as demand and pressures require
Record the outage, restart times and any equipment that failed to start

tasks.explanation: A stable supply and a correct lineup come before any start, because restarting into a wrong lineup can damage pumps or the system. Pressures and sounds prove a healthy start, and the record captures equipment that needs follow up.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for preparing a booster station for peak summer demand.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: seasonal readiness for one station serving an irrigation heavy area.

cards.label: Review last summer run times, alarms and any low pressure periods
Test each pump under load and confirm standby capacity
Service strainers, check valves and cooling or ventilation systems
Confirm chemical and fuel or backup power supplies for the season
Set the seasonal pump control settings and alarm call out roster
Record the readiness check and brief all shifts on the plan

tasks.explanation: Peak readiness is proven by testing every pump, including standby, before the peak arrives. Support systems and call out coverage fail more summer events than pumps do, so they are checked in the same pass and briefed to all shifts.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for checking surge protection at a pump station.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual check of surge vessels, relief valves and controls.

cards.label: Review the station surge events and pressure spike records for the year
Inspect surge vessel levels, pressures and bladder or air system condition
Test the pressure relief valve operation under the approved procedure
Check pump control settings for soft start and stop ramps where fitted
Correct any deficiency found and retest the device
Record the check and file the results with the station safety records

tasks.explanation: Surge records show whether protection has actually been called on. Each device is inspected and tested in turn, deficiencies are retested after correction, and the results are filed as safety records because surge protection protects the whole main.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a monthly backup power test at a pump station.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: generator test under load at one station.

cards.label: Notify dispatch and record station conditions before the test
Switch the station to backup power under the approved procedure
Run the duty pump on backup power and record pressures and run time
Check fuel level, coolant and battery condition during the run
Return the station to utility power and confirm normal operation
Log the test, fuel use and any defect and raise work orders for defects

tasks.explanation: The test proves the station can pump on backup power, not just that the generator starts. Running under load reveals fuel, cooling and battery weaknesses, and defects become work orders the same day.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a routine check of a booster chlorination feed at a pump station.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one chemical feed system at a booster station.

cards.label: Check the chemical storage level and record the amount on hand
Inspect feed lines, injection point and containment for leaks
Compare the feed rate setting with the station flow and target dose
Measure the residual downstream and compare it with the target
Adjust the feed only if the equipment checks are satisfactory
Record chemical use, feed setting and residual in the station log

tasks.explanation: Storage, lines and containment are checked before dose is judged, because leaks and low supply mimic dosing problems. The residual downstream is the proof of the feed, and the log ties chemical use to the water actually treated.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for locking out a pump for motor maintenance.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one pump isolated for contractor motor work.

cards.label: Notify operations and confirm the standby pump can carry the station
Transfer duty to the standby pump and confirm stable pressures
Isolate the pump suction and discharge valves and tag them
Lock out the motor electrical supply and apply personal locks and tags
Drain the pump casing and confirm zero energy before work starts
Record the lockout in the station log and brief the contractor on site rules

tasks.explanation: Standby capacity is proven before the duty pump is surrendered. Isolation, lockout and draining follow in energy order, zero energy is confirmed before hands go on the equipment, and the contractor is briefed so site rules are shared.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a quarterly pump station performance trend review.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: review for one station using run, energy and alarm records.

cards.label: Compile run hours, starts and energy use for each pump for the quarter
Compare energy per volume pumped with previous quarters
Review alarm counts and causes for repeat patterns
Check whether pump rotation kept run hours balanced
Identify the top maintenance or control improvement for the station
Present the trend review and the improvement plan to the supervisor

tasks.explanation: Trends reveal slow decline that daily checks miss. Energy per volume is the efficiency signal, repeat alarms point to root causes, and the review ends with one ranked improvement rather than a list nobody owns.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a cross connection survey of a commercial property.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one commercial building survey under the utility cross connection control program.

cards.label: Review the property water use and any existing backflow records before the visit
Walk the property with the owner contact and list all water uses and connections
Identify hazards such as boilers, irrigation, process water and hose connections
Match each hazard to the required protection for its hazard class
Issue the survey report listing required installations or tests
Set the compliance deadline and schedule the follow up check

tasks.explanation: Records before the visit focus the walkthrough. Every use is listed because the missed connection is usually the hazard, protection is matched to hazard class, and a deadline plus follow up turns a survey into compliance.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the annual routine that keeps backflow tester records current.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: program routine for all testers working in the system.

cards.label: List all testers who submitted reports in the past year
Verify each tester certification and test kit calibration record is current
Notify testers whose documents expire in the next quarter
Remove testers with lapsed documents from the accepted tester list
Update the program list used by customer service
File the routine check and the notices sent

tasks.explanation: Only current testers produce reports the program can accept. Checking calibration as well as certification matters because an accurate tester with an uncalibrated kit still produces unreliable results, and customer service works from the same updated list.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps in the program response to a failed backflow preventer test.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one failed test report received for a high hazard property.

cards.label: Verify the report details and the hazard class of the property
Notify the property owner that repair or replacement and a retest are required
Set the compliance deadline based on the hazard class
Record the failed device as non compliant in the program tracking system
Confirm the retest report shows a pass before the deadline
Escalate overdue high hazard cases to the supervisor for enforcement steps

tasks.explanation: High hazard failures get the fastest deadlines because the contamination risk is highest. The device stays flagged non compliant until a passing retest is in hand, and escalation follows the deadline, not a reminder cycle that drifts.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing backflow requirements for a new commercial service.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one new service application for a commercial building.

cards.label: Review the application for water uses planned in the building
Assign the hazard class from the highest hazard use identified
Specify the required premises isolation protection for that class
Notify the applicant of the requirement before the service is activated
Inspect or receive the test report for the installed device
Add the device to the program inventory with its test due date

tasks.explanation: Requirements are set from planned uses before the service goes live, because retrofitting protection after occupancy is slower and costlier. The device enters the inventory with a due date at installation, so the first test is never missed.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the spring irrigation backflow program routine.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: seasonal routine for residential and commercial irrigation systems.

cards.label: Send spring reminders to irrigation customers with test due notices
Confirm test reports received match devices in the program inventory
Follow up properties with overdue tests in hazard order
Check a sample of installations for unprotected hose or auxiliary connections
Update the inventory for removed or replaced irrigation devices
Report seasonal compliance rates to the supervisor

tasks.explanation: Spring is when irrigation systems are charged, so reminders and due notices go before startup. Sampling installations catches the unprotected connections that paperwork misses, and the seasonal compliance rate shows whether the routine is working.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for responding to a suspected backflow incident at a distribution site.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one report of discoloured water and pressure loss near an industrial property.

cards.label: Isolate the suspect property service if contamination is possible
Notify the supervisor and follow the provincial drinking water notification procedure
Collect samples at the property boundary and at nearby distribution points
Inspect the property backflow protection with the owner contact
Keep the service isolated until sample results and protection are satisfactory
Document the incident, results and corrective actions in the program file

tasks.explanation: Isolation comes first because protecting the public system outranks confirming the cause. Samples at the boundary and nearby points show whether anything entered the main, and the service stays isolated until both results and protection are proven.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for running the hydrant use permit and backflow routine.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: program routine for bulk water filling from hydrants.

cards.label: Issue the permit only for designated filling hydrants and approved equipment
Verify the applicant backflow preventer and meter are approved and tested
Record the starting meter reading at the first fill
Inspect permitted filling sites during the season for correct setup
Record final readings and bill the volume used
Review the season permits and revoke any permit with repeated violations

tasks.explanation: Designated hydrants and tested protection keep bulk filling from becoming a contamination or loss problem. Site inspections during the season catch setups that drift from the permit, and revocation for repeat violations gives the routine consequences.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the annual backflow device inventory audit.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: audit of the program device inventory.

cards.label: Export the device inventory and sort by hazard class and test due date
Compare inventory counts with test reports received during the year
Identify devices with no test report and no removal record
Visit or contact the highest hazard sites on the missing list first
Correct the inventory for removed, replaced and newly found devices
Report audit results and the overdue device count to the supervisor

tasks.explanation: The audit reconciles paper devices with tested devices. Missing reports on high hazard devices are chased first, field checks correct the inventory, and the overdue count is the program health measure management needs.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a residential cross connection education routine.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one seasonal campaign covering hose, pool and irrigation hazards.

cards.label: Select the seasonal hazards to feature, such as hoses in pools and chemical sprayers
Prepare plain language guidance with the utility contact for questions
Deliver the guidance with utility bills or the seasonal notice in the target area
Offer hose vacuum breakers or guidance at the utility office during the campaign
Track calls and questions received to judge which hazards need more work
Report the campaign results and next season focus to the supervisor

tasks.explanation: Education targets the hazards homeowners actually create each season. Plain guidance plus a contact produces questions the program can answer, tracking those questions shows which hazard to feature next, and the report closes the campaign.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the annual cross connection control program review.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: yearly review of surveys, testing and incidents.

cards.label: Compile survey, test and compliance counts for the year by hazard class
Review incidents and failed tests for common causes
Check tester list currency and inventory audit results
Identify property types with the lowest compliance for targeted surveys
Set next year survey and follow up targets from the findings
Present the review and targets to management for approval

tasks.explanation: The review is organized by hazard class because risk is not evenly spread. Low compliance property types become next year survey targets, and approved targets turn the review into the following year work plan.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for analysing main break records to find repeat break mains.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: five years of break records for the whole system.

cards.label: Compile break records with location, main material, size and age for each break
Map the breaks to show clusters by street and by main segment
Count breaks per segment and rank segments by break frequency
Compare the ranking with main age and material patterns
List the worst segments as candidates for renewal or closer monitoring
Present the analysis and candidate list to management

tasks.explanation: Break history only guides renewal when breaks are tied to specific segments. Mapping and counting reveal repeat segments that single break reports hide, age and material patterns explain the ranking, and the candidate list feeds capital planning.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing response performance after a major main break.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: review of one large break that flooded a commercial street.

cards.label: Reconstruct the timeline from first report to isolation, repair and restoration
Compare isolation time with the program target for a break of this size
Review customer notifications and complaint handling during the event
Check sampling and disinfection records for the return to service
Identify the step that caused the longest delay
Record lessons and update the break response procedure where needed

tasks.explanation: The timeline shows where time was actually lost, which is often isolation or notification rather than repair. Sampling records are reviewed with the same care as the repair, and the procedure is updated so the lesson changes the next response.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for investigating a winter cluster of main breaks in one area.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: several breaks in one neighbourhood during a cold snap in Manitoba.

cards.label: Map the break locations and the dates against the cold snap temperatures
Check the main material, depth of cover and frost depth for the area
Review pressure records for spikes during the cold period
Inspect one break site excavation for frost or bedding conditions
Rank the causes supported by the evidence collected
Recommend monitoring, pressure or renewal actions for the area

tasks.explanation: Cold weather breaks have several possible causes, so temperature, depth, pressure and site evidence are gathered before ranking them. Recommendations follow the supported cause, whether that is frost depth, pressure control or renewal.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing repair methods used on main breaks this year.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual review of clamp, sleeve and cut out repairs.

cards.label: List repairs by method, main size and material from the break reports
Compare return to service times and repeat failures by method
Review repair costs recorded for each method where available
Check which methods were used outside their suitable conditions
Update the repair method guidance for crews
Report the review findings to the supervisor

tasks.explanation: Methods are compared on outcomes in this system, not on preference. Repeat failures by method are the strongest signal, use outside suitable conditions is corrected in guidance, and crews get updated direction from the review.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for analysing customer impact from main breaks for the annual report.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one year of breaks analysed for outage impact.

cards.label: For each break, record customers affected and outage duration from the reports
Total customer outage hours by area and by month
Identify the breaks with the largest customer impact
Check whether notification reached affected customers before shutoff where planned
Recommend isolation or valving improvements for high impact areas
Include the impact analysis in the annual distribution report

tasks.explanation: Counting breaks alone hides their real cost, which is customer outage hours. The largest impact events get the attention, notification performance is checked honestly, and valving improvements are recommended where one break isolates too many customers.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a valve access improvement project arising from break analysis.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: valves that delayed isolation in recent breaks.

cards.label: List valves that were buried, paved over or inoperable during recent breaks
Prioritize the list by the isolation areas those valves control
Locate, raise or repair each valve box in priority order
Operate each valve to prove it can isolate its area
Update the valve records and isolation maps with the proven positions
Report project completion and remaining problem valves to the supervisor

tasks.explanation: Break reviews repeatedly show isolation delays come from valve access, not crew effort. Prioritizing by isolation area fixes the highest consequence valves first, and each valve is proven by operation before the map is trusted again.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for introducing cause coding to main break reports.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: new routine for all break reports from next month.

cards.label: Define the cause codes, such as corrosion, frost, third party damage and joint failure
Add the codes and a photo requirement to the break report form
Brief crews and supervisors on assigning a cause at the repair, not later
Review the first month reports for missing or inconsistent codes
Correct the coding guidance where crews found it unclear
File the routine and review coded causes quarterly

tasks.explanation: Cause data is only useful if it is assigned at the excavation, where the evidence is visible. A first month review catches inconsistent coding while the routine is new, and quarterly review turns codes into the patterns that guide renewal.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing emergency repair stock after the winter break season.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: clamps, sleeves, pipe and fittings stock review.

cards.label: Count stock used during the winter break season by size and type
Compare use with the stock levels held at season start
Identify any size that ran out or delayed a repair
Restock to the planned levels and add any size the season showed was missing
Check stored materials for damage and rotate stock as needed
Record the review and the new stock list in the stores system

tasks.explanation: Stock levels are set by what winter actually used, not by last year list. A size that delayed a repair is the strongest argument for holding it, damaged stock is removed before it fails on a night call, and the stores record matches the shelf.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for running a night main break response drill.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one unannounced style drill for the on call crew.

cards.label: Set the drill scenario and the safety limits with the supervisor in advance
Call out the crew through the normal dispatch process and start the clock
Have the crew locate the scenario valves on the map and in the field
Walk through isolation, notification and repair setup without breaking ground
Stop the drill and debrief response times and problems found
Record drill results and assign fixes for any gaps found

tasks.explanation: The drill tests the real call out path, not a classroom version. Map and field valve location is where night responses lose time, the debrief converts problems into assigned fixes, and the record proves the drill happened and mattered.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for prioritizing mains for renewal using break program data.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: renewal candidate list for the capital plan.

cards.label: Rank mains by break frequency from the break records analysis
Add condition factors such as age, material and consequence of failure
Combine break and condition scores into a renewal priority list
Check the list against planned road and development projects for coordination
Estimate renewal lengths for the top priority mains
Present the prioritized list for the capital plan

tasks.explanation: Break frequency leads the ranking because it is measured failure, while age and material add context. Coordinating with road projects saves restoration cost and disruption, and lengths turn a ranked list into a plannable capital program.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the supervisor daily operations review.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: morning review covering the previous day and the day ahead.

cards.label: Review overnight alarms, call outs and any adverse results
Check storage levels, pressures and pump station status for all zones
Review today planned work, isolations and customer notifications
Confirm crew assignments and any contractor work in the system
Flag any item needing management or provincial contact notification
Brief the crews and record the review decisions in the operations log

tasks.explanation: Overnight events are reviewed before the day plan, because an unresolved alarm changes what crews should do. Planned work is checked against system status, notifications are confirmed before isolations, and the log makes the decisions visible to the next shift.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a supervisor led debrief after a significant distribution incident.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: debrief within days of a major break or quality event.

cards.label: Collect the event records, timelines and sample results while they are fresh
Invite the responding crew, dispatch and any contractor involved
Walk the timeline and identify what helped and what delayed the response
Agree the specific procedure, stock or training changes to be made
Assign each change an owner and a completion date
File the debrief and check completion of the actions at the next review

tasks.explanation: Debriefs work while memory and records are fresh. Walking the timeline with everyone involved surfaces causes a single report misses, and owned, dated actions are what separate a debrief from a discussion.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the quarterly operator training and certification review.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: review for all distribution operators.

cards.label: List each operator certification class, expiry and required training
Compare the list with the certification levels the system requires on shift
Identify gaps where only one operator holds a needed qualification
Schedule training or exam preparation for the identified gaps
Update the training matrix and the shift coverage plan
Report the review and any coverage risk to management

tasks.explanation: Coverage risk appears when a needed qualification sits with one person. The matrix makes expiries and single points of failure visible early, scheduling follows the gaps, and management hears about coverage risk before it becomes a vacancy problem.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building the weekly distribution work plan.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one week plan covering maintenance, programs and reactive work.

cards.label: Collect overdue work orders and program tasks due this week
Add reactive items carried from last week break and complaint work
Check crew availability, contractor bookings and material stock
Sequence the work so isolations and notifications are grouped by area
Issue the plan to crews with the daily priorities marked
Review completion at week end and carry forward unfinished items with reasons

tasks.explanation: The plan starts from what is overdue and due, not from a blank page. Grouping isolations by area reduces customer disruption, daily priorities survive the week changes, and the week end review explains carry forward items instead of losing them.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a supervisor monthly safety inspection of distribution work.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: inspection covering one field crew and one facility this month.

cards.label: Select the crew task and facility to inspect from the monthly rotation
Observe the crew setup for traffic control, excavation and personal protective equipment
Check the facility for housekeeping, chemical storage and access control
Discuss findings with the crew on site and correct immediate hazards at once
Record the inspection and assign dated actions for other findings
Follow up the actions at the next monthly inspection

tasks.explanation: Observation in the field shows real practice, not paperwork practice. Immediate hazards are corrected on the spot, other findings get dated actions, and follow up at the next inspection is what makes the routine more than a tour.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for supervisor oversight of a contractor main installation.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one contractor installing a new main section.

cards.label: Review the approved drawings, disinfection plan and traffic plan before work starts
Confirm locates, permits and customer notifications are complete
Inspect tie in points and materials on site before installation begins
Visit during pressure testing and disinfection to witness key steps
Review test and sample results before accepting the main
Sign off acceptance and file the records with the asset information

tasks.explanation: Oversight starts before ground is broken, because drawings and plans are cheapest to correct then. Witnessing testing and disinfection protects the acceptance decision, and the main is accepted only on results, with records filed for the asset file.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the supervisor monthly operations budget tracking routine.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: monthly review of distribution operating costs.

cards.label: Collect the month costs for labour, materials, contractors and energy
Compare each category with the monthly budget and the year to date position
Investigate the largest variances and record the causes
Identify work that can be deferred or brought forward within the budget
Update the forecast for the remaining months of the year
Report the position and forecast to management

tasks.explanation: Variance investigation focuses on the largest items first, where the money actually moves. Deferral and acceleration decisions are made from the forecast, not from the month alone, and management gets the full year picture every month.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a supervisor audit of distribution operating records.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: quarterly audit of logs, sample records and work orders.

cards.label: Select a sample of weeks and pull the operations logs and sample records
Check records are complete, signed and filed in the correct location
Compare sample records with the laboratory reports for the same dates
Check work orders are closed with outcomes recorded, not just marked done
List gaps and assign corrections with dates
Report the audit and keep the findings with the quality records

tasks.explanation: The audit compares records with independent sources such as laboratory reports, because a complete looking log can still be wrong. Work order outcomes matter for asset history, gaps get dated corrections, and findings stay with the quality records for the next audit.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting the monthly on call roster.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: roster for operators and supervisor backup.

cards.label: List qualified operators available for on call duty in the month
Check leave, training and certification coverage for each week
Assign primary and backup call out for each week in rotation
Publish the roster to dispatch, crews and management
Confirm each operator has the current call out list and contact numbers
Record any swaps in the roster log so dispatch always has the current version

tasks.explanation: Qualification and leave are checked before names are placed, because an unavailable or unqualified on call operator is a gap discovered at the worst time. Publishing to dispatch and logging swaps keep the roster true after it is issued.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for preparing an operator annual performance review.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: preparation for one operator review meeting.

cards.label: Collect the operator work records, training completions and incident involvement
Review the records for achievements, gaps and development needs
Draft review points tied to specific work examples, not general impressions
Set development goals that match the training matrix needs
Hold the review meeting and record the agreed goals
File the review and schedule the mid year check on the goals

tasks.explanation: Reviews are prepared from records so they are fair and specific. Goals are tied to the training matrix so individual development also closes system coverage gaps, and a mid year check keeps the goals alive after the meeting.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the fall cold climate readiness program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: system wide preparation before freeze up in a Saskatchewan system.

cards.label: Review last winter freeze ups, breaks and hydrant drainage problems
Inspect and winterize hydrants, blow offs and exposed facilities
Check heat tapes, heaters and insulation at stations and chambers
Stock freeze response materials, thawing equipment and repair clamps
Brief crews on winter procedures and the frozen service response plan
Record readiness completion and any items carried into winter

tasks.explanation: Last winter problems set this fall priorities. Hydrants, heating and insulation are checked while repair is still easy, stock and briefings prepare the response side, and carried items are recorded so they are not forgotten once snow arrives.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for responding to a frozen customer service line.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one residential frozen service reported during a cold snap.

cards.label: Confirm the freeze is in the service line and not a main or internal plumbing issue
Check whether neighbouring services are also frozen, which suggests a wider problem
Record the service material, depth and any previous freeze history at the address
Thaw the service using the utility approved method for its material
Advise the customer on keeping a small flow or other approved prevention during the cold snap
Flag the address for the shallow or problem service list for follow up

tasks.explanation: Confirming the location of the freeze prevents wasted thawing and wrong advice. Neighbour checks reveal whether this is one shallow service or an area problem, the approved method protects the pipe material, and flagging the address builds the prevention list.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a winter main break response in extreme cold.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one break during a minus 30 degree cold period in Alberta.

cards.label: Confirm the break location and identify isolation valves from the map
Set traffic control and protect the work area from ice forming on the road
Close the isolation valves slowly and confirm flow at the break stops
Set up site heating and lighting for crew safety during the repair
Repair the main and restore flow slowly, checking the repair under pressure
Clear ice from the road and record the break, weather and repair details

tasks.explanation: Winter adds ice, heating and crew exposure to a normal break response. Traffic and ice control protect the public as well as the crew, slow restoration limits surge in cold brittle conditions, and weather details in the record help later winter analysis.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the program that checks hydrants after extreme cold periods.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: checks following a week of extreme cold.

cards.label: List hydrants in areas with known drainage or shallow main concerns
Visit each listed hydrant and check the barrel for standing water or ice
Pump out or thaw any hydrant found holding water, following the utility procedure
Mark hydrants that cannot be cleared as out of service and notify dispatch and fire contacts
Record the condition found for each hydrant visited
Schedule drainage repairs for the spring program from the records

tasks.explanation: The check list targets hydrants history says are at risk, rather than the whole system. A hydrant holding water is cleared or honestly marked out of service, because a frozen hydrant discovered at a fire is the failure this program exists to prevent.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for inspecting an elevated tank for ice damage after spring thaw begins.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one elevated tank after a severe winter.

cards.label: Review winter ice records and level trends for the tank
Inspect the exterior coating, roof and overflow for ice damage signs from the ground
Check the interior during the scheduled inspection or by camera where used
Inspect ladders, vents and the aviation light for ice related damage
List repairs by urgency, with any water quality risk first
Schedule the repairs and record the inspection in the facility file

tasks.explanation: Winter records tell the inspector where ice was worst. Exterior and interior checks cover both visible damage and hidden coating harm, water quality risks are repaired first, and the file record sets up next winter comparison.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for winterizing main blow offs and air valves before freeze up.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: fall visit to blow offs and air valves on exposed rural lines in British Columbia interior.

cards.label: Open each chamber and check for water, damage and insulation condition
Operate the blow off or air valve to confirm it works
Drain chamber water and clear the discharge line
Repair or replace insulation and chamber seals where damaged
Confirm the vent and drain paths will not freeze shut
Record the winterizing result for each site

tasks.explanation: Chambers are checked and operated before cold arrives, because a frozen blow off is discovered only when it is needed. Drainage and insulation protect the assembly, vent paths are confirmed open, and site records drive spring follow up.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a winter heating and freeze protection check at pump stations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: all booster stations before the coldest months.

cards.label: Check building heaters and thermostats and record setpoints
Inspect exposed piping, chemical lines and small diameter lines for insulation and heat tape operation
Test heat tape circuits and replace failed sections
Check standby heating arrangements for power outage periods
Seal drafts around doors and pipe entries found during the visit
Record the check and raise work orders for any failed protection

tasks.explanation: Small lines and chemical feeds freeze before mains do, so they get specific attention. Heat tape is tested, not assumed, outage heating is considered because freeze risk peaks when power fails, and failed protection becomes a work order before winter, not during it.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for spring thaw monitoring of the distribution system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: monitoring routine during the main thaw period.

cards.label: Identify areas with deep frost, shallow mains and past thaw related breaks
Increase pressure and flow monitoring in those areas during thaw
Inspect known problem sites for ground movement or leaking signs
Respond to the first thaw breaks with cause notes tied to frost conditions
Track break and freeze reports against falling frost depth
Close the monitoring period with a summary that updates the fall readiness list

tasks.explanation: Thaw is when frost movement breaks mains that survived the cold. Monitoring focuses where frost and history combine, cause notes during thaw are the evidence fall planning needs, and the summary feeds directly into the next readiness program.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing service line depths in a frost prone subdivision.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: review triggered by repeated frozen services on two streets.

cards.label: Compile freeze records by address for the subdivision
Compare recorded service depths with the local frost depth in severe winters
Check whether freezes cluster on services installed in a particular period
Recommend options such as insulation, depth correction at renewal or customer guidance
Prioritize the streets by freeze frequency and customer impact
File the review for use in renewal planning and customer advice

tasks.explanation: Repeated freezes on the same streets indicate a depth or installation pattern, not bad luck. Comparing depth with severe winter frost depth tests the explanation, options are matched to renewal timing, and the review stays on file so advice and planning use the same facts.

tasks.prompt: A district metered area in a Saskatchewan city shows minimum night flow of 14 L/s against a historic norm of 4 L/s, and the rise began in one week in February.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional DMA with 2,100 services in Regina area conditions. Night flow is measured between 02:00 and 04:00. Step testing and acoustic loggers are available.

evidence.label: Minimum night flow rose from 4 L/s to 14 L/s in one week and stayed there.
Step testing drops night flow by 9 L/s when one 600 m cast iron section is isolated, and by almost nothing elsewhere.
Acoustic loggers on that section correlate a strong leak noise between two hydrants 90 m apart.
Customer billed consumption in the DMA is unchanged over the same period.
A paired DMA on newer plastic mains shows no night flow change that week.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A leak on the isolated cast iron section is losing about 9 to 10 L/s at night
The whole city demand grew in one week and raised every DMA night flow
The DMA inlet meter began over registering in February
Residents across the DMA started running taps all night at the same time

inference.explanation: The step test isolates almost all of the rise to one section and loggers correlate leak noise there, while billed use is flat and a paired DMA is unchanged. A meter fault cannot produce a step test drop or leak noise, and city wide growth would lift the paired DMA too.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Excavate at the correlated noise midpoint after a pinpoint listening survey on the section
Replace the DMA inlet meter and recheck night flow next month
Lower DMA pressure by 100 kPa for the whole winter

nextClue.explanation: Pinpoint listening at the correlated location confirms the leak point before excavation, which is the direct confirmation of the step test result.

clueText.nc-a: Listening confirms the loudest noise at one joint, and excavation finds a split bell joint leaking into a storm drain.
clueText.nc-b: The inlet meter passes a later accuracy test, and a meter fault would not explain the step test drop.
clueText.nc-c: Lowering pressure would cut all use and risks fire flow, and it would not locate the leak the step test already isolated.

tasks.prompt: A Manitoba town suspects leakage because production rose 18 percent in a year, yet its district night flows look normal everywhere.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional town with one bulk meter at the plant outlet and four DMAs. Large meter testing equipment is available.

evidence.label: Minimum night flow in all four DMAs stayed at historic levels all year.
Billed customer consumption is flat year over year.
A volumetric tank drawdown test shows the plant bulk meter reads 9 percent high against the measured volume passed.
Acoustic survey of the oldest mains finds no leak noise above background.
The bulk meter is 14 years old and has never been accuracy tested.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A large trunk main leak is hiding between the plant and the DMAs
The apparent loss is a bulk meter over registration error, not real leakage
Customers across town are using 18 percent more water without it being billed
All four DMA meters failed low at the same time

inference.explanation: Night flows are normal in every DMA, no leak noise is found, and the drawdown test proves the bulk meter reads 9 percent high. A hidden trunk leak would raise at least one DMA or plant outlet night flow, and four meters failing together is not supported by any test.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Launch a town wide leak survey of every service connection
Remove and bench test or replace the bulk meter, then restate the water balance with the corrected factor
Raise treated water production reporting targets to match the meter

nextClue.explanation: Correcting the bulk meter fixes the input side of the water balance, which is where the measured error sits.

clueText.nc-a: A service survey cannot explain normal night flows in all four DMAs.
clueText.nc-b: After replacement, the same drawdown passes within 1 percent and the unexplained loss nearly disappears.
clueText.nc-c: Restating targets would hide a proven meter error instead of correcting the balance.

tasks.prompt: In an Alberta irrigation community, district night flow is high every summer but returns to normal each fall without any repairs.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional DMA serving homes and small acreages near Lethbridge. Night flow records cover three full years.

evidence.label: Night flow is 11 L/s from June to August and 3 L/s from October to April in each of three years.
Step testing in July shows the excess spread evenly across the DMA, with no single section dominating.
Several hydrants are found with caps loose and signs of recent use on summer mornings.
Daytime billed consumption also rises each summer with lawn and garden use.
Acoustic logging in July finds no concentrated leak noise.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: One large leak seals itself every fall and reopens every June
The DMA meter drifts with warm weather each summer
Seasonal summer night use, including hydrant and irrigation draws, explains the high summer night flow
A trunk main leak runs only when the river level is high

inference.explanation: The pattern repeats on a seasonal cycle for three years, the excess is spread evenly rather than isolated to one section, hydrants show use, and no leak noise is found. A leak does not seal and reopen on a calendar, and a meter drift would not match loose hydrant caps and higher billed summer use.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Excavate the oldest main in the DMA during July
Replace the DMA meter each spring as a precaution
Log hydrant use permits and sample night flows on streets with and without irrigation timers for two weeks

nextClue.explanation: Comparing night use street by street tests the seasonal use explanation directly and separates permitted draws from any true leakage.

clueText.nc-a: Excavation has no target, since step testing found no dominant section.
clueText.nc-b: The meter reads the same seasonal pattern as street level logging, so it is recording real flow.
clueText.nc-c: Streets with timed irrigation account for most of the summer night flow, and permitted hydrant use explains the rest.

tasks.prompt: After a deep cold snap and rapid thaw near Saskatoon, one district night flow doubles and a faint hissing is reported near a river crossing.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional DMA with a cast iron river crossing installed in the 1970s. Frost depth that winter reached well below normal.

evidence.label: Night flow doubled in the week after the thaw and stayed doubled.
Step testing isolates most of the increase to the 300 m section containing the river crossing.
Ground above the crossing stays wet and soft while surrounding ground dries after the thaw.
Pressure in the DMA is normal and customer use is unchanged.
A paired DMA away from the river shows no night flow change.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Spring runoff raised groundwater and the DMA meter is reading groundwater inflow
Every customer in the DMA began thawing frozen services that week
The treatment plant raised zone pressure and opened an old leak across town
A frost and thaw related failure at or near the river crossing section is leaking

inference.explanation: The increase isolates to the crossing section, the ground above it stays wet, and a paired DMA is unchanged. Meter inflow is not possible in a pressurized main, customer thawing would not isolate to one section, and no pressure change is recorded.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Run acoustic correlation across the crossing section and inspect the crossing chambers at both banks
Wait until summer to see if the night flow recovers on its own
Replace all service lines in the DMA

nextClue.explanation: Correlation across the suspect section plus chamber inspection directly tests the crossing failure the step test points to.

clueText.nc-a: Correlation peaks at a cracked joint just before the crossing, and the chamber shows fresh washout gravel.
clueText.nc-b: A doubled night flow with wet ground will not recover on its own and delay risks undermining the crossing.
clueText.nc-c: Service lines are spread across the DMA and step testing cleared their sections.

tasks.prompt: A district in Winnipeg shows high night flow, but step testing finds no section where isolation lowers the flow.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional DMA containing a hospital, two schools, and homes. A full step test was done on two separate nights with the same result.

evidence.label: Night flow holds at 9 L/s all night instead of dipping to a low minimum.
Isolating each of six sections in turn changes night flow by less than 0.5 L/s each time.
Flow falls to 2 L/s on the one statutory holiday night in the test period, then returns to 9 L/s.
The hospital laundry and sterilizer schedule runs from 23:00 to 05:00 on working nights only.
Acoustic loggers across the DMA record no leak noise.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Legitimate institutional night use, mainly the hospital schedule, explains the high night flow
Six separate leaks of equal size are hidden in the six sections
The DMA meter reads a steady false 7 L/s all night
A large leak sits exactly at the DMA inlet where step testing cannot see it

inference.explanation: No section isolation changes the flow, there is no leak noise, and the flow collapses on the holiday night when the hospital schedule stops. Six equal leaks and a steady meter error would not follow a working night calendar, and an inlet leak would still appear when downstream sections close.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Excavate each of the six sections in turn looking for leaks
Meter the hospital service for one working week and subtract its night profile from the DMA balance
Declare the DMA leakage as 7 L/s and add it to the loss target

nextClue.explanation: A dedicated service meter measures the suspected legitimate use directly, which is what a leakage calculation must remove first.

clueText.nc-a: Excavation has no target because no section changed the flow when isolated.
clueText.nc-b: The hospital service accounts for about 6.5 L/s through the night, leaving a true minimum near the historic norm.
clueText.nc-c: Calling it leakage without measuring the hospital draw would overstate loss and misdirect the repair budget.

tasks.prompt: A prairie city lowers pressure in one district at night as a trial, and leakage falls sharply while customer use barely changes.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional DMA with a pressure reducing valve that can be scheduled. Night pressures and flows were logged for two weeks before and during the trial.

evidence.label: At 420 kPa night pressure, minimum night flow is 10 L/s with estimated customer night use of 2 L/s.
At 300 kPa night pressure, minimum night flow falls to 5.5 L/s with the same estimated customer use.
Daytime pressures and billed consumption are unchanged by the night only trial.
Known leak repairs in the DMA in the past year were mostly joint weeps and service leaks, not bursts.
A neighbouring DMA held at full pressure shows no night flow change in the same weeks.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: One large burst is throttling itself at lower pressure
Much of the district leakage is pressure dependent background leakage from many small joint and service weeps
Customers use far less water at night when pressure drops
The inlet meter under registers at lower pressure

inference.explanation: Customer night use is accounted for and flat, the fall is large and gradual in character, and past repairs show many small weeps rather than one burst. A single burst would have been found as a dominant step test drop, and the control DMA rules out a seasonal or meter wide effect.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Search for one large burst with a full acoustic survey first
Raise night pressure to find leaks faster by sound
Adopt scheduled night pressure control for the DMA and track leakage against pressure over the next quarter

nextClue.explanation: Sustained pressure management with tracking tests whether the pressure and leakage relationship holds, which is the Class 2 program decision this case supports.

clueText.nc-a: Past step tests and repair history already show no single dominant leak to find.
clueText.nc-b: Raising pressure would increase loss from the many small weeps the records describe.
clueText.nc-c: Over the quarter, leakage tracks night pressure closely and total loss falls by about a third with no pressure complaints.

tasks.prompt: A reservoir fed district in British Columbia shows a steady overnight reservoir drop that is larger than the metered outflow to the district.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional ground reservoir feeding one district by gravity. Staff ran a test with the district outlet closed for one night under supervision.

evidence.label: With the outlet open, the reservoir drops 0.90 m overnight while district meters total a volume equal to a 0.55 m drop.
With the outlet closed all night, the reservoir still drops 0.20 m with no district demand.
Evaporation and temperature effects for the covered reservoir are estimated at under 0.01 m per night.
The reservoir outlet meter passes a drawdown accuracy check.
Dye and level checks find no overflow, since the overflow line stays dry all night.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: District customers use far more water at night than their meters record
The reservoir level sensor overstates the overnight drop
Water is leaving the reservoir or its feed main by a path other than the metered district outlet, such as a reservoir or trunk leak
The reservoir overflows quietly every night

inference.explanation: The closed outlet test still loses 0.20 m with no demand, overflow is dry, evaporation is negligible, and the outlet meter is proven accurate. Customer under recording cannot explain a loss with the outlet shut, and a sensor error would not match the metered open outlet shortfall pattern.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Isolate reservoir cells and the feed main in turn overnight to find which element loses level with everything shut
Recalibrate all district customer meters
Raise the reservoir operating level to cover the loss

nextClue.explanation: Element by element isolation with everything shut is the direct test for which structure or main is losing water.

clueText.nc-a: The feed main section loses pressure in isolation while both cells hold level, locating the loss to the trunk main.
clueText.nc-b: Customer meters cannot cause a drop with the district outlet closed.
clueText.nc-c: Raising the level adds stored volume but does not find or stop the loss.

tasks.prompt: Minimum night flow in a new district metered area in Alberta is high from the first month, even though the mains are new plastic pipe.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional DMA commissioned eight months ago near Edmonton. Boundary valves were set at commissioning and not checked since.

evidence.label: Night flow is 8 L/s in a DMA where new pipe leakage should be near 1 L/s.
Step testing inside the DMA finds no section that lowers the flow.
A listening test on one boundary valve hears water passing while the valve shows closed.
Fully seating that boundary valve in a trial drops night flow to 1.5 L/s the same night.
The neighbouring older DMA night flow fell slightly in the same period.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: New plastic mains leak heavily along every joint
New homes in the DMA use eight times the expected night flow
The DMA meter was installed backwards
A boundary valve is passing, so the new DMA is quietly feeding part of the neighbouring district at night

inference.explanation: New mains do not leak evenly at this rate, step testing inside the DMA finds nothing, and a passing boundary valve is heard and then proven by the trial seating that restores normal flow. A reversed meter would misread direction, not create a flow that a valve trial removes.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Pressure test every new main in the DMA again
Seat and tag all boundary valves, then add boundary valve checks to the DMA monthly routine
Replace the DMA meter with a larger size

nextClue.explanation: Boundary valve verification closes the proven transfer path and the routine check prevents the balance error from returning.

clueText.nc-a: The mains passed commissioning tests and step testing cleared them again.
clueText.nc-b: With boundaries verified, both DMAs report stable and separate night flows for the next month.
clueText.nc-c: Meter size does not explain flow that stops when a boundary valve is seated.

tasks.prompt: A large recreation complex in a Manitoba city is suspected of inflating district water loss, because district daytime use is high but night flow is normal.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional DMA with one large metered recreation complex. The complex meter is a 15 year old turbine meter.

evidence.label: District night flow is at the historic norm, so background leakage looks low.
The water balance still shows high unexplained daytime loss in the DMA.
A test of the recreation complex meter at low and medium flows shows it under registers by 22 percent.
At high test flows the same meter is within 3 percent of true volume.
The complex irrigates and fills pools mostly at low to medium flow for long hours.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The complex meter under registers at the low flows it runs at most, creating apparent daytime loss
A daytime only leak opens when the complex is busy
District customers waste water only in daytime
