The DMA inlet meter over registers only in daytime

inference.explanation: Night flow is normal, the balance gap is daytime, and the meter test shows a large low flow error exactly where the complex operates for long hours. A daytime leak would show in step testing and would not match a proven meter error curve.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Run a full DMA leak survey during complex operating hours
Bill the complex a flat estimated charge and stop metering it
Replace or resize the complex meter for its real flow range and restate the DMA balance

nextClue.explanation: Correcting the meter at its operating range removes the measured error that creates the apparent loss.

clueText.nc-a: A leak survey does not address a meter proven to under register at working flows.
clueText.nc-b: Flat billing hides consumption and removes the data the balance depends on.
clueText.nc-c: With a correctly sized meter, recorded complex use rises and the DMA unexplained loss falls to near the night flow estimate.

tasks.prompt: Step testing a Saskatchewan district over three nights shows small flow drops at almost every step instead of one large drop.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional DMA of mixed age housing in Moose Jaw. Each of nine sections was isolated in turn on comparable nights.

evidence.label: Each isolation step lowers night flow by 0.4 to 0.9 L/s, and the steps add up to most of the excess night flow.
No single section accounts for more than a tenth of the excess.
Acoustic loggers hear faint noise at many points rather than one loud source.
Repair history for the DMA lists many service line weeps found over past years.
Customer night use was measured separately and is too small to explain the pattern.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: One large leak sits on a section that was never isolated
The district loss is many small service and joint leaks spread across the DMA, not one main leak
The step test valves all leak past their seats equally
Night flow rises because the whole DMA pressure rises at night

inference.explanation: Every section was isolated, each contributed a similar small drop, loggers hear many faint sources, and history matches many service weeps. One large hidden leak contradicts the even step pattern, and passing step valves would blur, not create, consistent section by section drops.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Plan a service renewal and targeted repair program by section rather than a single excavation
Excavate the oldest section first and expect the loss to end
Repeat the step test until one large drop appears

nextClue.explanation: A section by section renewal program matches the proven distribution of many small leaks and can be tracked by repeating night flow after each section.

clueText.nc-a: After the first two sections are renewed, night flow falls by about the amount those steps predicted.
clueText.nc-b: One excavation cannot fix losses measured in all nine sections.
clueText.nc-c: Repeating the same test will reproduce the same even pattern, not create a single drop.

tasks.prompt: Large meter testing across a Manitoba city finds its oldest turbine meters accurate at high flow but losing registration steadily at the low flows their sites now mostly run.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional testing programme in a Winnipeg area system covering forty large meters at three flow rates each. Site flow profiles were logged before testing.

evidence.label: At high test flow, the oldest meters average within 2 percent of true volume.
At low test flow, the same meters average 14 percent under registration.
Most of their sites now run at low flow for over 80 percent of hours after process changes reduced their peaks.
Newer meters tested the same week hold accuracy across all three flow rates.
District balances containing the oldest meters show the largest apparent losses.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The test bench reads low flow incorrectly for old meters only
The sites are leaking at low flow in proportion to meter age
Customers with old meters are bypassing them at night
Wear in the oldest meters has eroded their low flow accuracy, and their sites now live at low flow, creating apparent loss

inference.explanation: The same bench tests newer meters accurately at low flow, the error follows meter age and wear, and site profiles prove the meters spend their lives where they now err. Leaks would appear in night flow checks, not in bench tests of removed meters.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Programme replacement or resizing of the oldest meters by their site flow profiles, starting with the largest apparent loss districts
Retest the oldest meters at high flow only and return them
Adjust all old meter readings up by a flat 14 percent

nextClue.explanation: Sizing meters to real site profiles fixes registration where the water actually flows, and district balances verify the recovery.

clueText.nc-a: The first replacement group cuts its district apparent loss by about half in the following quarter.
clueText.nc-b: High flow only testing certifies the one range the sites rarely use.
clueText.nc-c: A flat adjustment ignores that error varies by flow and by meter.

tasks.prompt: Winter night flow in a mobile home park district in Alberta is high every cold month, then normal all summer, for three winters running.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional DMA serving a mobile home park near Red Deer. Park services are shallow and the park operator manages frost protection taps.

evidence.label: Night flow rises to 7 L/s whenever the temperature stays below minus 20 C for several days.
Park staff confirm frost protection bleed taps are opened park wide during deep cold and closed in spring.
Metered flow at the park master meter matches the DMA excess closely on cold nights.
Step testing in summer finds no leak sections.
No burst repairs were needed in the park in any of the three winters.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The park mains burst every winter and heal every spring
Cold weather makes the DMA meter over register
Frost protection bleed taps running through cold periods explain the winter night flow
Residents fill bathtubs nightly only in winter

inference.explanation: The excess matches the master meter, follows deep cold exactly, and park staff confirm bleed taps are opened by policy, while summer step testing finds no leaks. Bursts do not heal seasonally, and a meter error would not match the park master meter and staff records.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Excavate park mains each winter looking for bursts
Record bleed tap use as legitimate winter night use in the DMA balance and review tap settings with the park operator
Count the full winter excess as leakage in the annual audit

nextClue.explanation: Treating measured frost protection flow as legitimate use keeps the leakage figure honest and focuses attention on whether tap settings can be reduced safely.

clueText.nc-a: Three winters produced no bursts to excavate, and step testing cleared the mains.
clueText.nc-b: With bleed use logged nightly, the winter leakage estimate returns to the summer baseline.
clueText.nc-c: Counting known frost protection flow as leakage would overstate loss and misstate the audit.

tasks.prompt: A city in British Columbia finds its annual non revenue water jumped in the year it changed from bimonthly to monthly customer meter reading.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility that changed reading cycles mid year. Production metering did not change. The audit compares calendar year production to billed volumes by read date.

evidence.label: Production for the calendar year is unchanged from the prior year trend.
District night flows and leak repair counts are unchanged year over year.
Billed volume in the transition year excludes about one month of consumption that was used but read in the next year.
When billed volumes are matched to the months the water was actually used, the loss percentage returns to the prior level.
Customer meter accuracy testing that year shows no change in fleet accuracy.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Leakage doubled in the transition year and then recovered
Customer meters across the city slowed down for one year
Production meters over registered for exactly one year
The jump is a billing lag accounting artifact from the reading cycle change, not new physical loss

inference.explanation: Physical indicators, night flow, repairs, production trend, and meter accuracy are all unchanged, and realigning billed volume to use month removes the jump. Real leakage doubling would move night flow and repair counts, which it did not.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Launch an emergency leak detection program for the transition year pattern
Replace the customer meter fleet based on the audit jump
Restate the audit on a use month basis and note the cycle change in the water balance method

nextClue.explanation: Fixing the accounting basis corrects the audit without field work, and the method note prevents the same artifact at the next cycle change.

clueText.nc-a: Field programs cannot fix a gap that disappears when volumes are aligned by use month.
clueText.nc-b: Fleet testing already showed accuracy was unchanged that year.
clueText.nc-c: The restated audit matches the prior three years within one percentage point.

tasks.prompt: During a one night reservoir isolation test in a Manitoba district, staff close the district feed to measure true night demand, but the reservoir keeps falling.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional test in a Brandon area district. The feed valve was proven tight by a pressure hold test earlier that day.

evidence.label: With the feed valve closed and proven tight, the reservoir still falls at a steady rate all night.
District pressure holds steady all night from a second feed that staff did not know was open.
Mapping later finds an old intertie valve to a neighbouring zone shown as abandoned on current drawings.
Closing that intertie in a second test stops the reservoir fall when the feed is closed.
No overflow or drain flow is observed during either test.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: An undocumented open intertie is supplying the district during the test, so the reservoir fall is real outflow through that path
The reservoir is leaking through its floor at a steady rate
The feed valve leaks despite passing its hold test
The district uses no water at all at night and the fall is evaporation

inference.explanation: District pressure holding steady with the feed shut proves another supply path exists, and closing the found intertie stops the fall. A floor leak would continue after the intertie closes, and the feed valve passed a hold test the same day.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Survey, tag, and set the intertie to its intended normally closed position, and correct the system drawings
Line the reservoir floor to stop the steady fall
Repeat the feed valve hold test weekly until it fails

nextClue.explanation: Correcting the intertie position and the drawings fixes both the test error and a real zone boundary problem.

clueText.nc-a: The next isolation test shows the reservoir holding level and the district pressure falling as expected with no supply.
clueText.nc-b: Lining the floor does not explain district pressure holding with the feed shut.
clueText.nc-c: The valve already passed its hold test, and the intertie closure removed the fall.

tasks.prompt: A Saskatchewan district shows leakage concentrated in its daytime balance, yet acoustic surveys keep finding nothing and night flow is only slightly high.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional DMA in Prince Albert with a large food plant on a dedicated service. Plant production runs two day shifts.

evidence.label: Night flow is only 1 L/s above the historic norm.
Daytime DMA inflow exceeds billed daytime use by about 12 L/s during plant shifts.
The gap disappears on plant shutdown weekends while homes use water normally.
A check meter on the plant service records about 12 L/s more than the plant billing meter during shifts.
The plant billing meter is oversized for its current reduced production flows.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A leak runs only during plant shifts and stops on weekends
The plant billing meter under registers at its current flows, creating apparent daytime loss
Plant staff steal water through an unmetered bypass that a check meter would also miss
Home meters across the DMA all under register in daytime

inference.explanation: The check meter on the same service measures the missing flow, the gap follows plant shifts exactly, and night flow is near normal. A shift timed leak is not supported by any acoustic or step result, and a bypass before the check meter is ruled out because the check meter was placed at the service entrance and captured the flow.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Survey all DMA mains acoustically during plant shifts
Replace the plant meter with a correctly sized compound or modern meter and verify with the check meter for one month
Add the gap to the DMA leakage total in the annual report

nextClue.explanation: Correct meter sizing at the proven error point restores the balance, verified against the check meter.

clueText.nc-a: Surveys already found nothing because the water is metered plant use, not leakage.
clueText.nc-b: After replacement, billing and check meters agree within 2 percent and the daytime gap closes.
clueText.nc-c: Reporting meter error as leakage would misstate both loss and plant consumption.

tasks.prompt: Two neighbouring districts in an Alberta city are compared for a renewal budget: one has high night flow per kilometre of main, the other has high total night flow but far more mains.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional paired DMA comparison prepared for capital planning in Calgary area conditions. Both DMAs were measured in the same month with the same method.

evidence.label: District A loses 0.9 L/s per kilometre at night across 8 km of main.
District B loses 0.3 L/s per kilometre at night across 40 km of main.
District A mains are 60 year old cast iron, while District B mains are mostly 25 year old plastic.
Break records per kilometre are also three times higher in District A.
Customer counts per kilometre are similar in the two districts.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: District B should rank first because its total night flow is larger
Both districts are equal because both lose water at night
District A has the worse leakage intensity and should rank first for renewal despite its smaller total loss
District A loss is explained by having more customers per kilometre

inference.explanation: Per kilometre loss and break rate are both far higher in A, customer density is similar, and A has the older leak prone material. Total flow alone favours the much larger district and hides intensity, which is what renewal ranking should compare.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Rank renewal by total night flow only and schedule District B first
Split the budget equally because both districts lose water
Rank renewal by loss per kilometre and break rate, and schedule District A first with a post renewal night flow target

nextClue.explanation: Intensity based ranking directs renewal to the worst performing mains and sets a measurable target for the work.

clueText.nc-a: Total flow ranking would spend first where mains are newer and loss per kilometre is lowest.
clueText.nc-b: Equal splitting ignores the threefold difference in both loss intensity and breaks.
clueText.nc-c: The plan funds District A first and its target is a night flow intensity at or below the District B level within two years.

tasks.prompt: A district in Winnipeg reports rising leakage each spring for five years, always recovering by midsummer after a repair program finds one or two service leaks.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional DMA with many galvanized services near end of life. Spring thaw in Manitoba brings frost movement in the service trenches.

evidence.label: Each spring, step testing finds one or two sections with fresh leak flow that was absent the prior fall.
Repairs each spring are on service lines at the frost depth zone, with split or pulled joints.
Main break counts in the DMA are flat across the five years.
Night flow returns to baseline after each spring repair round.
A neighbouring DMA with copper and plastic services shows no spring pattern.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The trunk main is cracking a little more each spring
Spring runoff enters the DMA meter chamber and adds false flow
Customers irrigate heavily each spring and stop by midsummer
Seasonal frost movement is failing aging galvanized services each spring, creating a repeating spring leakage rise

inference.explanation: Repairs land on services at frost depth each spring, mains are flat, the pattern is absent where services are modern materials, and flow returns to baseline after service repairs. A trunk main failure would appear in break counts and would not be cured by service repairs.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Program spring step testing each year and accelerate galvanized service renewal in the DMA
Replace the trunk main through the DMA
Ignore the spring rise because it recovers by midsummer

nextClue.explanation: Planned spring testing plus service renewal attacks the proven repeating failure point instead of reacting each year.

clueText.nc-a: After half the galvanized services are renewed, the spring rise is about half its former size.
clueText.nc-b: The trunk main has a flat break record and spring repairs never touch it.
clueText.nc-c: Ignoring the rise leaves real treated water leaking for months each spring.

tasks.prompt: A low lying zone in a British Columbia interior city loses pressure every afternoon while the high zone above it stays normal.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional two zone system in Kamloops area conditions. The low zone is fed through one pressure reducing valve station.

evidence.label: Low zone pressure falls to 150 kPa each afternoon and recovers each evening.
High zone pressure stays near 550 kPa through the same afternoons.
The reducing valve outlet gauge reads near zero flow pressure drop at low demand but the valve is found almost fully closed with a broken spring in its pilot.
Opening the station bypass in a supervised trial restores low zone afternoon pressure at once.
No main breaks or large demands were recorded in the low zone that week.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The pressure reducing valve has failed toward closed and is starving the low zone at demand
The high zone is using all the water before it reaches the low zone
The low zone elevated tank is too small for afternoon demand
Afternoon heat expands air in the low zone mains and blocks flow

inference.explanation: The valve pilot spring is broken, the valve sits almost closed, and the bypass trial restores pressure immediately, while the high zone stays normal. Tank size and high zone use cannot explain instant recovery through a bypass around one valve.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Add storage to the low zone before checking the station
Repair the reducing valve pilot and spring, then log low zone pressure through the next afternoon peak
Raise the high zone pressure to push more water down

nextClue.explanation: Repairing the proven failed component and logging the next peak verifies control is restored under the condition that failed.

clueText.nc-a: Storage would mask a failed valve and the bypass trial already located the fault.
clueText.nc-b: After repair, the valve holds its setpoint and afternoon pressure stays above 320 kPa.
clueText.nc-c: Higher upstream pressure against a closed valve adds stress without restoring control.

tasks.prompt: Pressures in a Saskatchewan zone swing up and down by 120 kPa every few minutes all day, and customers hear pipes humming.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone fed through a pressure reducing valve station in a Saskatoon area system. A fast pressure logger was placed downstream of the station.

evidence.label: The logger shows a repeating cycle: pressure climbs, then drops sharply, with a period of about four minutes.
The reducing valve is heard hunting, opening and closing in time with the pressure cycle.
Zone demand during the swings is steady, with no large user cycling.
The valve pilot sensing line is found partly plugged with scale, cleaned in a trial, and the cycle period lengthens at once.
A second zone fed from the same high zone through a different station is steady.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Customers across the zone open and close large taps in a four minute rhythm
A partly plugged pilot sensing line makes the reducing valve hunt and cycle zone pressure
The zone tank level is bouncing and driving the swings
The pressure logger is faulty and inventing a cycle

inference.explanation: The valve hunts in time with the logged cycle, demand is steady, a sister zone is steady, and cleaning the sensing line changes the cycle at once. Coordinated customer rhythm is not credible, and a faulty logger would not match valve sounds or respond to pilot cleaning.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Replace the zone pressure logger and close the case
Tell customers the humming is normal for this zone
Clean and flush the pilot system fully, then log downstream pressure for a full day to confirm steady control

nextClue.explanation: Full pilot cleaning plus a day of logging verifies the valve now holds pressure steadily, which is the operating requirement.

clueText.nc-a: The logger agreed with valve behaviour and with the trial result, so it was reporting a real cycle.
clueText.nc-b: A 120 kPa swing is not normal and risks fatigue damage to services and fixtures.
clueText.nc-c: After full cleaning, downstream pressure holds within 15 kPa for the full day.

tasks.prompt: A hilltop area in Alberta has poor pressure that began the week a new pressure zone boundary was commissioned nearby.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional hilltop area in a Red Deer area system. Zone boundaries were redrawn and two boundary valves were operated during commissioning.

evidence.label: Hilltop pressure fell from 340 kPa to 190 kPa in the commissioning week and stayed there.
Streets just below the hilltop, moved to the new low zone, have normal pressure for that zone.
One boundary valve between the hilltop and the high zone is found closed, though the commissioning plan shows it open.
Opening that valve in a trial restores hilltop pressure to 335 kPa.
No demand growth or breaks occurred on the hilltop that week.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The new low zone is stealing the hilltop supply through the boundary
Hilltop homes need individual booster pumps from now on
The hilltop was cut off from its high zone feed by a boundary valve left closed at commissioning
The hilltop main suddenly tuberculated during commissioning week

inference.explanation: Timing matches commissioning, the plan shows the valve open while it is found closed, and a trial opening restores pressure fully. Tuberculation does not occur in a week, and individual boosters are not needed once the intended feed is restored.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Open and verify the boundary valve, then audit every boundary valve position against the commissioning plan
Install booster pumps at hilltop homes at utility cost
Move the hilltop into the low zone permanently

nextClue.explanation: A full boundary audit prevents other commissioning errors from hiding elsewhere in the redrawn zones.

clueText.nc-a: The audit finds all other valves as planned, and hilltop pressure holds normal for a month.
clueText.nc-b: Boosters treat a valve position error as a design problem and add cost without need.
clueText.nc-c: The low zone cannot serve the hilltop elevation at adequate pressure, as its own setpoint shows.
